Pedal pushers
PED-ul PUSH-erz
noun (Silent Generation slang)
American name of the 1940s and 1950s for calf-length women’s trousers, originally worn for bicycle riding — cut short so they would not catch in the chain or the pedals, hence the name. In use by the 1940s, they became a casual summer staple of the 1950s, worn with flat shoes and a blouse for picnics, gardening, and errands; the same cut is now usually called capris.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Pedal pushers came into Grandma’s closet in the 1950s: cotton slacks cut off at the calf, first for riding a bicycle without catching the hem in the chain, then for picnics, gardening, and Saturday errands. They were practical and cool in July, and for the time a little daring; some mothers thought a lady ought to wear a skirt to the grocery store. Families still remember the arguments. Scripture does not hand us a pattern book, but it does give principles for dress. The first is modesty: women are to "adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9). The second is that outward things are not the main thing: "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning" (1Pe 3:3), but "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4). The third is freedom from anxiety about clothes, for our Lord said of the lilies, "That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mat 6:29). A grandmother can tell her granddaughter honestly that styles change every decade, that modesty does not, and that the loveliest clothing God gives is the robe of His Son’s righteousness. Within those bounds a Christian family can choose with a clear conscience, and pedal pushers on a bicycle in 1956 were a cheerful example of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, 1940s–50s; first for bicycle riding) for calf-length casual women’s trousers — a practical summer fashion, judged by Scripture’s abiding rule to adorn themselves in modest apparel (1Ti 2:9).

expand to see more

PEDAL PUSHERS, n. pl. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) Calf-length casual trousers for women and girls, originally designed for bicycle riding. "She wore her pedal pushers and saddle shoes to the church picnic."

Decode for families: what Grandma called pedal pushers you might call capris; styles change, modesty doesn’t.

Key Scripture

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

1Pe 3:3 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;"

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Mat 6:29 — "And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."

Modern Corruption

A practical, wholesome garment-word with little to correct; it simply raises the abiding question of modesty that every generation’s fashion must answer.

expand to see more

Pedal pushers names a sensible garment for a bicycle and a summer day, and there is no sin in the word. The arguments families once had over them are a reminder that every age wrestles with what is fitting, and good-hearted Christians did not always agree.

The abiding rule is not a hemline but a heart: modest apparel, shamefacedness, and sobriety (1Ti 2:9), with the inward ornament prized above the outward (1Pe 3:4). A family that teaches the principle will be ready for each new fashion; a family that teaches only a list will be out of date in ten years.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin pes, pedis (foot) → pedal (foot lever) + pusher → pedal pushers (1940s), cyclists’ trousers → 1950s casual summer wear.

expand to see more

Latin pes, pedis — foot; pedal, a lever worked by the foot

Latin pulsare via French pousser — to push

1940s: pedal pushers, calf-length trousers for bicycle riding

1950s: a casual summer staple; later called capris
